_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-15) first version. The alias rule is told as the depot's provider's own, unnamed: Anthropic's Model IDs and versioning page (read 15 October 2026) describes moving aliases only for its models before the 4.6 generation, and says every model ID, dated or dateless, is a pinned snapshot. Every number comes from the sim's stated groups: the labelled 200 (60 urgent: 24 ice, 36 other; 140 routine) and last night's 96 (52 ice, 44 other), with each snapshot's answer per group. Timeline: launch and the test set in January 2026; last change and last test run 3 September (58 of 60); notice emailed 30 September to an unread inbox; 9 October 05:58 the school-hill report sent now by the old snapshot; alias moved 18:00 on 14 October; the same words at 21:14 marked next round; the post is written on the morning of 15 October.
title: The Night It Changed Its Mind
setting: a weathervane that turns on still nights

post.author: u/gritter_night_blodwen
post.title: I'm the night controller at a county's winter roads depot. Nobody has changed our app since September. On the first hard frost, the same words that got a gritter sent last Friday were told to wait for the morning round.

blocks.text: I'm Blodwen, night controller at Hurlestone, Brackmoor County's winter roads depot. On cold nights I'm alone in the control room. I send out our seven gritters, lorries that spread salt on icy roads. The drivers say that when the weathervane on our roof turns on a still night, something is wrong.

The public text us reports, like "ice on the hill by the school, a car's in the hedge." Since January an assistant sorts each one for me: send a gritter now, which we call urgent, or wait for the next round, our 04:00 run. It runs on a language model, a program that reads text and writes text back (a1e01). We rent it from a provider, a company that runs models.

Each report goes to the model with our prompt: the standing instructions sent first, saying what counts as urgent and asking for one of the two answers. My screen shows each answer and how many reports tonight are urgent.

Every change to the app goes in our change log, a list of who changed what and when. At launch, Aloysius, our developer, and the day supervisor marked 200 old reports by hand: 60 urgent, 140 not. That is our test set, reports with the right answers agreed in advance (a5e01). It runs before any change goes live (a5e05). The app must find at least 57 of the 60, and send no more than 10 of the 140 by mistake.
The last entry in the log is 3 September: a new bypass added to the routes, test set 58 of 60. Nothing since.
Two lines from the app's record, each showing the date and time, the report, and the answer:

09 Oct 05:58  "Ice on the hill by the school, a car's in the hedge."  URGENT
14 Oct 21:14  "Ice on the hill by the school, a car's in the hedge."  NEXT ROUND

The same words. Svea lives by the school and copied her own text from Friday. Wednesday was the first hard frost of the year. A gritter reached that hill on the 04:00 round. Nobody was hurt, but a second car had slid into the hedge by then.
At 21:30 I went out to the yard. The vane was turning. There was no wind.

This morning Aloysius found an email from the provider, sent on 30 September to the old roads office address nobody reads. Our app never asks for one fixed version of the model. It asks by a short name, fieldfare-2, that the provider points at its newest version. That kind of short name is called an alias.

Each model version is a snapshot: the model frozen as it was on one date, like one printing of a book, with a full name ending in that date. At 18:00 on 14 October the alias moved from fieldfare-2-20251118 to fieldfare-2-20260929.
The old one still answers to its full name until it retires, switched off for good, on 14 April 2027.
So Aloysius ran the test set, and last night's 96 reports, through both, calling each by its full name.

diagram.aria: Aloysius's drawing. The depot app asks for fieldfare-2, with no change log entry since 3 September. The alias fieldfare-2 pointed at the snapshot fieldfare-2-20251118 until 18:00 on 14 October: test set 58 of 60, and 31 of last night's 96 urgent when rerun. From 18:00 it points at fieldfare-2-20260929: test set 47 of 60, and 17 of last night's 96 urgent.

blocks.caption: Drawn from Aloysius's runs this morning. Until 18:00 on 14 October the alias meant the November 2025 snapshot, which finds 58 of the test set's 60 urgent reports. From 18:00 it meant the September 2026 one: 47. Last night's 96 went through the new one, which marked 17 urgent. The old one marks 31 of the same 96 urgent. So 14 that the old one would have sent now went to the next round. Svea's is one.

blocks.text: Nobody here chose an upgrade, and nobody touched the prompt. The model changed, and nobody shipped anything: no change of ours went live. Tonight will be colder. What do we change before I'm on at 18:00?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Vanes turn for wind you can't feel on the ground. Your app's wind is up at the provider. Two words you may want. The share of truly urgent reports a model finds is called recall: 58 of 60 is about 97 in 100, and 47 of 60 about 78. A model's answers shifting over time while your own app stays the same is called drift. Case a5e05 was an upgrade a team chose on purpose; a6e08 was a prompt edited with no version kept. Yours is neither. Two questions. What makes your test set run, and when did it last? And when the alias moved, who was meant to hear about it?

replies.author: u/gritter_night_blodwen
replies.text: It only runs when we change something, so 3 September. The notice went to the old inbox. Aloysius says it gave the date of the move and the old snapshot's retirement. It also said that even a fixed version can shift slightly when the provider changes its own machinery around the model, which it calls an infrastructure update.

comments.author: u/always_latest_wilburga
comments.text: Newer is always better. The alias keeps you on the provider's best model without lifting a finger; that's what it's for. The other way is to pin: ask for one dated snapshot by its full name, every time. Then you're frozen on last year's model until the provider switches it off. One odd answer on one night is noise. Keep the alias and keep an eye on your urgent count.

replies.author: u/gritter_night_blodwen
replies.text: Last winter our hard-frost nights had between 12 and 35 reports marked urgent. Wednesday had 17.

comments.author: u/school_hill_svea
comments.text: That was me, both times. On Friday only our hill had frozen, and a gritter came in twenty minutes, so on Wednesday I sent the same words. I watched from the window as the second car went in. The driver climbed out and waved at me. Why did it believe me on Friday and not on Wednesday?

replies.author: u/gritter_night_blodwen
replies.text: I'm sorry. Aloysius could add a line to the prompt tonight: treat every report of ice as urgent. Or I could read every report myself. Around the radio and the drivers I can read and sort about 10 an hour. Wednesday brought 22 between 21:00 and 22:00.

reply.prompt: The night will be colder and Blodwen is on at 18:00. What should the depot change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep the model's alias so it stays current, and watch the urgent count more closely.
options.verdict: The next move is silent too
options.part2: Aloysius left the alias alone and set an alarm for any hard-frost night outside last winter's 12 to 35 urgent reports. He replayed Wednesday through it first: 17 urgent, inside the range, no alarm. The 14 reports that went to the next round sat inside a normal-looking count, Svea's among them. The count rises and falls with the weather, so it can't tell a model that misses ice from a night with less ice. The new snapshot was never run on the test set, and the alias still points wherever the provider sends it next. The vane turned again at 22:00.
options.senior: An alias is handy because someone else decides when your model changes, and that is also its danger. A count of answers can't measure quality: it moves with the weather, and a drop in recall hides inside a normal total. Only labelled answers show drift. Ask for a fixed version, and change it only on purpose, after your own test set passes.

options.text: Add a line to the prompt telling it to treat every report of ice as urgent tonight.
options.part2: Aloysius added the line at 17:00 and nobody ran the test set. On Friday morning he did: with the line, the new snapshot finds 58 of the 60 urgent reports, but sends 34 of the 140 routine ones now, where the bar allows 10. Wednesday's 96, replayed with the line, give 59 urgent against the old snapshot's 31: frost on parked cars and icy footpaths among them, far more than seven gritters can reach before the 04:00 round. The line traded missed ice for false alarms, and the alias can still move under it.
options.senior: A prompt change made to patch a model change is still a change, and it needs the same test run before it goes live. Here it swapped missed ice for false alarms: 58 of 60 found, but 34 routine reports sent now. And it leaves the alias in place, so the next snapshot may read the same line differently.

options.text: Have the night controller read and sort every public report by hand from now on.
options.part2: I sorted every report myself, around the radio and the drivers, about 10 an hour. Replayed that way, Wednesday's 96 pile up in the busy hours: 22 came between 21:00 and 22:00 and 18 in the next hour, so by midnight 22 were waiting, the last about 2 hours 12 minutes behind. A report like Svea's would have waited in that line. The busy hours are the frost hours, when waiting costs most. And the model is still on the alias for the day the depot wants it back.
options.senior: A person checking every answer can suit rare, high-stakes work, but not one person against a rush. Here the hand line peaks at 22 waiting on the worst night. Keep the model, fix its version, and spend people's time on the labelled answers that tell you whether to trust it.

options.text: Pin the exact model version, and switch only when the depot's own test set passes.
options.part2: At 10:00 Aloysius changed one line: the app now asks for fieldfare-2-20251118 by its full name, and he wrote it in the change log. He ran the test set on the new snapshot again: 47 of 60, below the bar of 57, so the switch is blocked. Replayed through the pinned version, Wednesday's 96 give 31 urgent, Svea's among them. The set now also runs every Monday at 09:00 on the pinned version, and the first run, on 19 October, gives 58 of 60. That run is how we would see an infrastructure update shift it. The old snapshot retires on 14 April 2027, so a version that passes must be found before then, and the provider's notices now come to the control room. At 21:30 the vane was still.
options.senior: Pin the exact version so your model changes only when you change it, and log it like any other change. Before any switch, run your own labelled test set on the new version and switch on purpose only when it passes your bar; here 47 of 60 blocks it. Keep running the set every week on the pinned version, because providers say behaviour can still shift slightly without a new version. And watch retirement dates: pinning delays an upgrade, it doesn't cancel it.

sim.title: Check the depot's model for drift
sim.lede: You're Aloysius with the depot's two sets. No real model runs here: every report belongs to a stated group, and each snapshot's answer for each group is in the table. The labelled 200: 60 urgent (24 about ice, 36 other) and 140 routine (30 about ice, 110 other). The old snapshot, fieldfare-2-20251118, finds 23 of the 24 urgent ice reports and 35 of the 36 others; the new one, fieldfare-2-20260929, finds 13 and 34. Both send the same 4 routine reports now. Last night's 96 have no labels: 52 about ice, 44 other. The prompt line's effect is stated: every report that mentions ice is marked urgent. The bar for a switch: at least 57 of 60 found, at most 10 of 140 routine sent now. The weekly eval runs the 200 on Mondays at 09:00 on the version in use; its infrastructure update is stated: one urgent ice report flips to next round on the old snapshot. By hand, about 10 reports an hour. The alias rule here is the depot's provider's. You open at 17:59 on 14 October, the alias on the old snapshot.
sim.tryThis: Try this: move the alias to the new snapshot and read 47 of 60 and 11 changed, with nothing in the change log. Switch to last night's 96: 17 urgent, 14 changed. Pin the old snapshot and see the move change nothing. Try a switch, turn on the ice line, and run the weekly eval on the alias and on the pinned version. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the depot changed. The app asked for its model by an alias, and at 18:00 on 14 October the provider pointed that alias at a new snapshot, which finds 47 of the test set's 60 urgent reports where the old one found 58. Last night it sent 14 reports to the next round that the old one would have sent now.

steps.title: An alias is a pointer, and pointers move.
steps.text: The depot's provider keeps each version of the model as a snapshot with a full dated name, like fieldfare-2-20251118. An alias is a short name that points at one of them. First the app sends its request to fieldfare-2. Then the provider looks up which snapshot the alias points at today. Then that snapshot answers. When the provider moves the alias, the next request goes to the new snapshot, with nothing changed in the app or its change log. What can go wrong: the notice goes to an inbox nobody reads, and the first sign is a wrong answer on a hard night. This is drift the team didn't cause: the model changed and nobody shipped anything. In a5e05 a team chose an upgrade; in a6e08 a prompt was edited with no version.

steps.title: Count what was found, by hand.
steps.text: Recall is the share of truly urgent reports the model finds. It needs labels: reports whose right answer people agreed in advance. Take the 60 urgent in the test set. The old snapshot finds 58: 58 / 60 is about 97 in 100. The new one finds 47: 47 / 60 is about 78 in 100. Split by kind, the loss is mostly ice: 23 of 24 ice reports against 13 of 24. Count the other mistake too, routine reports sent now: 4 of 140 on both. What can go wrong: a total can't show this. Last night's 17 urgent looked like an ordinary frost night, because the count moves with the weather.

steps.title: Pin the version, and write it down.
steps.text: Pinning means asking for one snapshot by its full dated name. First change the one line that names the model. Then record it in the change log like any other change, with the test set's result. From then on the model changes only when you change it. What can go wrong: a pinned snapshot still retires. This one is switched off on 14 April 2027, and after that every request to it fails, so pinning delays an upgrade; it doesn't cancel it.

steps.title: Switch on purpose, after the test set passes.
steps.text: When a new snapshot arrives, run the labelled set on it, calling it by its full name, before anything goes live. Compare the result with the bar: at least 57 of 60 found, at most 10 of 140 routine sent now. If it passes, switch, log it, and watch the first nights. If it fails, stay pinned and fix the cause, perhaps with a prompt change, which goes through the same test. Here the new snapshot gets 47 of 60, so the switch is blocked; with the ice line it gets 58 of 60 but sends 34 routine reports now, so that is blocked too. What can go wrong: 200 reports can't hold every kind of night, so add each real miss to the set.

steps.title: Run the set every week anyway.
steps.text: A pinned version's weights, the numbers it learned, don't change, but the provider's machinery around it can. Anthropic's page says infrastructure updates occasionally produce minor differences in behaviour. So run the same set on a schedule, here Mondays at 09:00, and compare with last week. In the sim a small stated update flips one report: 57 of 60, still a pass, but the weekly run shows 1 changed. What can go wrong: a weekly run on the alias would only have caught the move on Monday 19 October, five frost nights late.

diagram.aria: The fix. The depot app asks for fieldfare-2-20251118 by its full name: pinned, retiring 14 April 2027, and run on the test set every Monday, 58 of 60. A new snapshot, fieldfare-2-20260929, has to go through the test set gate first, which needs at least 57 of 60 found and at most 10 of 140 routine sent now. It gets 47 of 60, so it is blocked and never reaches the app.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for tonight. The app asks for the old snapshot by its full name, so a moved alias can't reach it. A new snapshot comes in only through the test set gate: at least 57 of 60 urgent found and at most 10 of 140 routine sent now. fieldfare-2-20260929 gets 47 of 60 and stays out. The same set runs on the pinned version every Monday at 09:00.

fix.title: The fix: pin the version, test before any switch, and test every week
fix.text: Change the app to ask for fieldfare-2-20251118 by its full name, and record that in the change log. Before switching to any new snapshot, run the depot's labelled 200 on it and switch only when it reaches the bar: at least 57 of 60 urgent found, at most 10 of 140 routine sent now. fieldfare-2-20260929 gets 47 of 60, so the depot stays where it is. Run the same set every Monday on the pinned version and compare with last week, report by report. Send the provider's notices to an address the control room reads, and plan the switch well before the old snapshot retires on 14 April 2027.

limits: A test set sees only what is in it. 200 reports from past winters may not include a new kind, like reports from the new bypass, so add every real miss to the set and keep its answers agreed by people.
Pinning has an end date. The old snapshot retires on 14 April 2027; if no version passes the bar by then, the depot has to accept a weaker one knowingly or change the prompt and test again.
A weekly run catches a shift up to a week late, and a small shift can stay inside the bar. Compare this week's answers with last week's report by report, not only the totals.

explain.seniorTake: If your app names its model by something the provider can repoint, your app can change without a deploy. Pin the exact version, record it like code, and treat every switch as a release: run your own labelled set first, compare it with an agreed bar, and switch on purpose when it passes. Keep running that set on a schedule even when nothing changed on your side, because the machinery around a fixed version can still shift, and watch retirement dates so a forced switch never arrives untested. Counts of answers are not evals; only labelled answers show drift. And read how your own provider names models: on Anthropic's current models every ID is already a fixed snapshot, and its page calls the belief that a dateless ID always means the latest a common misconception.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: a model ID is a pinned version
realWorld.text: Anthropic's Model IDs and versioning page says each Claude model ID identifies a pinned version of the model, and when you use a model ID in an API request, the underlying model remains constant for the lifetime of that ID. When an updated version is available, it ships under a new model ID.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: aliases for earlier models move
realWorld.text: For models before the 4.6 generation, the page says an alias such as claude-sonnet-4-5 is a convenience pointer that resolves to the most recent dated snapshot for that minor version. The depot's fieldfare-2 works like that kind of alias.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: dateless does not mean latest
realWorld.text: The page calls it a common misconception that dateless model IDs behave as evergreen pointers that route to the latest or best-performing version. From the 4.6 generation, the dateless ID maps to a single, fixed model snapshot.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: the machinery around the model can change
realWorld.text: The page says model weights are fixed for a given ID, but the serving infrastructure around the model can change, and that infrastructure updates occasionally produce minor differences in observable behavior even when the model ID and weights have not changed. It adds that every model ID has its own deprecation and retirement schedule.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: retirement dates in the lineup
realWorld.text: The models overview gives each current model a retirement commitment, such as not sooner than September 22, 2027 for Claude Opus 5.5, and notes that every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot, including the dateless IDs used from the 4.6 generation on.

realWorld.title: Chen, Zaharia and Zou, 2023: the same name, different answers
realWorld.text: Comparing the March and June 2023 versions of GPT-4, the paper reports that GPT-4 (March 2023) was reasonable at identifying prime vs. composite numbers (84% accuracy) but GPT-4 (June 2023) was poor on these same questions (51% accuracy). It concludes that the behavior of the same LLM service can change substantially in a relatively short amount of time, highlighting the need for continuous monitoring of LLMs.

asked: How do you handle a provider's new model version?
What is model drift and how would you catch it?
interview.answer: I pin the exact model version in configuration, by its full name, and record it in version control like any other change, so the model changes only when we change it. Some providers offer short names that move to the newest snapshot; others, like Anthropic's current models, make every ID a fixed snapshot; I check which before trusting a name. When a new version arrives, I treat it as a release: run our own labelled eval set on it, compare it with a bar agreed in advance, for example recall on the cases that matter most and a ceiling on false alarms, look at every answer that changed, and switch on purpose only if it passes, then watch the first days. Drift is the model's answers shifting while our code stays the same: a moved alias, a new version, or small changes in the provider's serving infrastructure. I catch it by running the same labelled set on a schedule, weekly for example, on the pinned version and comparing with last week's answers, because counts and averages move with traffic and hide it. I also track retirement dates and route provider notices to a team inbox, so a forced switch is planned and tested months ahead.

terms.def: A council's base for keeping roads safe in winter: salt stores, gritters and a control room. Hurlestone is Brackmoor County's.

A lorry that spreads salt, often mixed with grit, so ice melts or never forms. Hurlestone has seven.
The depot's planned 04:00 gritting run. A report marked next round waits for it instead of getting a gritter now.
A report that should get a gritter sent now. The depot's test set has 60 urgent reports and 140 routine ones.
A pointer on a roof that turns to show where the wind comes from. Hurlestone's turns on still nights.
A program that reads text and writes text back, one likely word at a time, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown huge (a1e01).
A company that runs language models and rents their use to others, through an API.
The agreed way one program asks another for something, like an order form at a counter. Providers offer one for their models.
The standing instructions sent to the model first, before the report itself. The depot's says what counts as urgent and asks for one of two answers.
A list of every change made to a system: who, what and when. The depot's last entry is 3 September.
To put a change live, so the people using the system get it. Nobody at the depot shipped anything after 3 September.
One fixed state of a model. Providers keep each as a snapshot with its own full name.
A model frozen as it was on one date, like one printing of a book. Its full name ends in that date, as in fieldfare-2-20251118.
A short model name, like fieldfare-2, that the provider points at one of its snapshots and can move to a newer one. Anthropic's page describes these for its earlier models.
The name an app sends to ask for a model. On Anthropic's current models it has no date and is still one fixed snapshot.
The second number in a model's name, as the 5 in Claude Sonnet 4.5. Anthropic's earlier aliases point at the newest snapshot within one minor version.
To ask for one snapshot by its full name every time, so the model changes only when you change it (a5e05). It delays upgrades; it doesn't stop them.
When a provider switches a snapshot off for good; requests to it then fail (a5e05). The depot's old snapshot retires on 14 April 2027.
Swapping the model behind a feature for a newer version (a5e05). There a team chose it; at the depot the provider made it.
The provider's email announcing a change: here, the date the alias moves and the date the old snapshot retires.
The depot's 200 past reports with the right answer agreed in advance by people: 60 urgent, 140 routine. A golden set (a5e01).
A fixed list of real inputs with the right answers agreed in advance, kept to score every version of a system (a5e01).
Inputs with the right answers marked in advance by people, kept to score every version (a5e05). The depot's test set is one.
The result a test must reach for a change to go ahead (a5e01). The depot's: at least 57 of 60 urgent found, at most 10 of 140 routine sent now.
The share of truly urgent items a model finds: found divided by labelled urgent. Old snapshot 58 / 60, about 97 in 100; new 47 / 60, about 78.
A routine report sent now as if urgent. Both snapshots make 4 on the depot's test set; with the ice line, 34.
A model's answers shifting over time while your own app stays the same: a moved alias, a new version, or the provider's machinery.
A test of what a model says: an input with a known right answer and a rule that marks the reply (a5e05). Like an exam with a mark scheme.
An eval suite run on every change to catch things that used to work and now don't, the way unit tests do for code (a5e05).
Running the same test set on a schedule, here Mondays at 09:00, on the version in use, and comparing with last week's answers.
A change the provider makes to the machinery around a model, such as how requests are routed, not to the model itself. It can still shift answers slightly.
The numbers a model learned in training. For a given pinned version they don't change.
An AI company that runs the Claude models. Its Model IDs and versioning page is this case's source on aliases and pinned versions.
A language model from OpenAI. Chen, Zaharia and Zou compared its March and June 2023 versions on the same questions.
A whole number above 1 that divides only by 1 and itself, like 7. Numbers that divide otherwise, like 9, are composite.
Short for large language model: a language model trained on a huge amount of text, the kind providers rent out.
A system that keeps every version of a project's files with who changed what and when, so any change can be found or undone (a5e05).
The international standard for information security management. Annex A 8.32 covers change management; 5.22 covers monitoring and managing changes to suppliers' services.
An audit report on a service company's controls, against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC8.1 covers authorising, testing and approving changes.

atWork: Look for any feature that names its model by a short name whose meaning someone else controls: a 'latest' tag, a family name with no date, a setting copied from a quick-start guide. It is a common pattern, and on providers where such names move, behaviour changes with nothing deployed. Ask four things. Which exact version does each feature use today, and is it in version control or the change log? Who receives the provider's notices, and does that inbox still exist? Do we have a labelled set with an agreed pass bar, and does it run before any switch and every week on the pinned version? When does our pinned version retire, and who owns finding its replacement? Check how your provider names versions too: on Anthropic's current models every ID is already a fixed snapshot. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control 8.32, change management, expects changes to information processing facilities and information systems to follow change management procedures, and control 5.22 expects you to monitor, review and manage changes in suppliers' services; a provider repointing an alias is such a change. If you report under SOC 2, criterion CC8.1 expects changes to be authorised, tested and approved before they are put in place; a model version nobody chose or tested would likely be a finding. Building the pinned version and the test run in from the first design costs far less than adding them after an audit, or after a frost.

recall.prompt: Your team's support app summarises customer emails with a model it calls by the provider's short name support-latest. Nothing has been deployed for six weeks, but since Tuesday staff say the summaries leave out refund amounts. What probably happened, and what would you change so it can't happen silently again?

keyIdeas.idea: The short name is an alias the provider moved to a newer model version
Pin the exact version by its full dated name
Run a labelled test set before any switch, and on a schedule

recall.model: The short name is probably an alias, and the provider moved it to a new snapshot, so the model changed while nothing was deployed. I'd pin the exact version by its full dated name and record it in version control. Then I'd build a labelled set of past emails with the refund amounts marked, run it on the pinned version and on the new one, and switch only when the new one passes an agreed bar. I'd also run it every week on the pinned version, since behaviour can still shift slightly, and send the provider's notices to an inbox someone reads.

recall.prompt: The depot's test set has 60 reports labelled urgent and 140 routine. A new snapshot marks 47 of the urgent ones urgent, and 4 of the routine ones too. What is its recall on urgent reports?
recall.why: Recall is urgent found divided by urgent labelled: 47 / 60, about 78 in 100. 47 of 200 divides by every report, 51 of 60 counts the 4 false alarms as finds, and 47 of 51 is the share of its urgent answers that were right, a different measure.

recall.prompt: A clinic's booking assistant has been pinned to one dated model version for a year, and its labelled set of 300 questions passed every week. This Monday the run shows 3 answers changed since last week, though nobody at the clinic changed anything and the version name is the same. The provider has also announced that the version retires in four months. What do you make of the change, and what do you plan?

keyIdeas.idea: A fixed version can still shift slightly when the provider's serving machinery changes
Read the changed answers one by one against the bar, and keep the weekly run
Before it retires, test the replacement on the same set and switch on purpose

recall.model: The version name is the same, so the weights are likely unchanged; a small shift like this usually comes from the provider's serving infrastructure around the model. I'd read the 3 answers one by one, check whether the set still clears the pass bar, and keep running it weekly. For the retirement I'd start now: run the same 300 questions on the replacement version, fix what fails, and switch on purpose well before it retires, logging the change.

recall.prompt: At 18:00 on 14 October the depot's app began sorting reports with a different snapshot, though its change log has no entry since 3 September. What changed?
options: The provider moved the alias fieldfare-2 to a newer snapshot
The old snapshot retired and requests fell back to another
The provider retrained the old snapshot in place
recall.why: The app asks for fieldfare-2, an alias, and the provider pointed it at fieldfare-2-20260929 at 18:00. Nobody deployed anything, the old snapshot retires only on 14 April 2027, and a pinned version's weights are never changed in place.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. We stayed pinned all winter, and the Monday run passed every week: 58 of 60, and 57 of 60 once in January after an infrastructure update (we read the one changed report and carried on). Now it's March, and the old snapshot retires on 14 April. The provider's newest snapshot, fieldfare-2-20260302, on our test set: 59 of 60 urgent found, but 15 of the 140 routine reports sent now. Aloysius says it's the best recall we've ever had, and with the deadline close he wants to switch tonight.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Should the depot switch tonight, and what should it do before the old snapshot retires?

keyIdeas.idea: It fails the bar on false alarms: 15 of 140 is over 10, so don't switch as it is
Fix the cause and run the same set again, switching on purpose before the retirement date
Look at the 15 routine reports it sends now, and treat any prompt fix as a logged, tested change

coldCase.model: Not tonight. 59 of 60 is better recall, but 15 of 140 routine reports sent now fails the bar, which allows no more than 10: on a frost night those are gritters sent to frosted cars while real ice waits. Look at the 15 and see what they share. If a prompt change fixes them, record it in the change log, run the set again on the new snapshot with the new prompt, and switch on purpose once it passes, before the retirement date. Keep the Monday run going on whichever version you end on.
